title: Choosing Your System
tagline: A retired engineer who recited a hundred thousand digits of pi, and how to choose the right number system for the job.
card: A feat of memory and a decision guide: five number systems side by side, and which one to use for a phone number, a year or a long code.
goal: you will compare the five number systems from this part, choose the right one for a given job, and combine more than one in the same session.

left_off.q: What does PAO stand for, and how many digits does one scene hold?
How do you assemble 341526 in PAO?
left_off.a: Person of 34, action of 15, object of 26.

left_off.q: Why avoid giving two PAO entries the same object?
left_off.a: The pictures would leak into each other.

text: In 2006, in a public hall in Japan, a retired engineer named Akira Haraguchi sat down to recite the number pi, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, which goes on forever and never repeats. He kept going for hours, with short breaks, far into the night.

By the time he stopped, he had reportedly said a hundred thousand digits, over about sixteen hours. The record was widely reported. It was not officially certified by the record-keeping organisation, so we have to say 'reported'. But nobody doubts that he knew a very large number of digits.

check.a: He recited pi from memory, to a hundred thousand digits, over about sixteen hours.

parts.talk: What is the longest number you have ever tried to remember? How did you do it?

text: How did he do it? Japanese is helpful here. In Japanese there is a long tradition of making numbers into words by sound. Each digit can be read in several ways, so a string of digits can be turned into syllables, and the syllables into words and stories. According to what he said afterwards, Haraguchi turned the digits into stories made of such words, and he learned them in small groups until they were automatic.
That is just what you are learning. The number becomes words, and the words become a story. The details are different, but the idea is the same.

check.q: What is the idea behind his method?
check.a: He turned digits into words and stories, learned in small groups, rather than trying to hold the bare digits.

parts.talk: Which of the four systems you know most resembles his method?

text: But notice what Haraguchi's feat does not tell us. It does not tell us that everyone should learn a hundred thousand digits. Most of us need a phone number, a PIN, a year, a code of ten digits on a parcel. For those jobs the best system is the one that is quickest for the job in front of you.
You now have five. In this lesson you put them side by side and learn to choose. A good memory athlete, like a good carpenter, has more than one tool and knows which one to pick up.

check.q: What is the lesson of this lesson?
check.a: Choose the number system that suits the job; do not use the biggest tool for a small task.

parts.talk: Which of your own numbers (phone, PIN, birthday) would you be happy to keep in your head for good?

words.m: a very difficult thing that someone does well. A feat of memory.
to say aloud from memory. He recited a poem.
to officially confirm that something is true. The record was never certified.
according to what people say, but not proved. He reportedly said a hundred thousand digits.
to join two or more things together. Combine two systems.
to be right for someone or something. Choose the system that suits the job.

source: Akira Haraguchi's 2006 recital is reported in the press; the figure has not been officially certified. Our own summary.

method.x: Every system turns digits into pictures. They differ in how much each picture can hold, how long they take to build, and what they are best at.

method.title: One number, five ways
lines: Candle, sailboat, balloon, swan: a candle burning on a sailboat tied to a balloon and pulled by a swan.
Bun, door, vine, shoe: a bun jammed in a door with a vine growing out of a shoe.
14 = TIRE, 92 = BONE: a giant tyre bounces on an enormous bone.
14 = A. D. (Anthony Daniels) doing the action of 92 = N. B. (Napoleon, one hand inside his coat).
Needs six digits: add two more (say 18) and use person, action, object.
method.pic: The same year, held by one scene of four things or by one person with one action, depending on the tool.

items.h: Ask how long the number is.
items.x: Up to four digits: shape, rhyme or Major. Longer: Dominic or PAO.

items.h: Ask how long you need to keep it.
items.x: Till tonight: any quick system. For good: build a scene you will return to.

items.h: Ask what you have already built.
items.x: Use the list you know best. A half-built list is slower than a simple one.
Years in Major; a long code in PAO; an ID number by shape. Choosing is part of the skill.

method.x:
small number, small tool.
long number, big tool.

Many people mix the Major System for single words with PAO for long strings, so that a number of any length can be handled. There is no rule. What matters is that you can decode your own pictures without hesitation.
Choose the system you would use for your own phone number, and explain why, in one minute.

try.title: Which system?
try.prompt: Match each job to the system you would choose first.
pairs: A four-digit PIN to remember till Friday
Twenty years and dates for a history exam
A twelve-digit number to keep for a month

items.s: One Dominic scene (person + action) holds ___ digits.
The shape and rhyme systems hold ___ digit(s) per picture.

try.title: Encode 3071 two ways
try.prompt: Encode 3071 using the Major System (30 and 71) and using the shape system (heart, ring, cliff, candle). Write both scenes.
try.model: Major: 30 = m + s: MOUSE or MASS; 71 = k + t: CAT or COAT. A giant mouse in a cat's coat. Shape: a heart rolls through a ring and jumps off a cliff holding a candle. Which one feels quicker to you?
checks: The Major words have the right sounds.
The shape scene has all four pictures in order.

try.title: A number of your own
try.prompt: Choose a number that matters to you (at least eight digits). Choose a system and write the scenes. Say why you chose it.
try.model: There is no single answer. Look for: right system for the length, scenes that are vivid, and one sentence saying why.

try.q: A friend must remember a four-digit PIN for tonight only. What do you advise?
opts: Build a hundred-person PAO list first
A quick shape or rhyme scene
try.why: A short number for a short time needs a quick tool. Save the big systems for the long numbers.

try.title: Defend your choice
try.prompt: Tell a partner, or yourself, which system you will mainly use, and when you would switch to another one.

cards: 1 digit per picture. Ten pictures that look like the digits.
1 digit per picture. Ten pictures whose names rhyme with the digits.
A word of 1 to 3 consonant sounds per picture. Vowels are free.
4 digits per picture: one person plus another person's action.
6 digits per picture: person, action, object.
Short number, short time: quick system. Long number: bigger system.

quiz.q: Which system holds the most digits in one picture?
quiz.why: PAO holds six; Dominic four; rhyme one.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for a four-digit PIN for tonight?
quiz.why: A quick simple system is enough.

quiz.q: Why is it important to be able to decode your own pictures?
opts: So you can turn a picture back into digits without hesitation
So other people can read them
quiz.why: A picture you cannot decode is useless.

quiz.q: Can you mix systems in one session?
quiz.why: Mixing is normal. Choosing is part of the skill.

challenge.title: Memory challenge: pi to fifteen digits
challenge.intro: The first fifteen digits after the 3 in pi are 3.14159 26535 89793. Learn them in five groups of three: 141, 592, 653, 589, 793. Use whichever system you like.
challenge.study: Five groups, five scenes (or one story). Do not just repeat the digits.

look_back.q: In PAO, which pair gives the object?
What are the Dominic letters for 6, 7, 8, 9?
Why are numbers hard to remember?
look_back.a: Numbers are not pictures, so the mind has nothing to hold on to.
